actions.justification: Patient presents with bilateral ankle edema and dyspnea — assess volume status to confirm congestion (wet vs dry) before initiating diuretic therapy, per AHA HF guidelines initial assessment.

Classify hemodynamic profile (warm vs cold) to determine appropriate treatment strategy — WET/WARM supports diuresis alone, WET/COLD may require inotropes. BP 138/82 suggests adequate perfusion but formal assessment is required.
BNP or NT-proBNP is a key diagnostic marker for heart failure severity and guides management. Per AHA guidelines, natriuretic peptides are required in initial HF assessment.

AHA guidelines strongly recommend echocardiography to confirm HFrEF diagnosis, assess LVEF, and evaluate structural abnormalities. This is the gold standard for HFrEF diagnosis and is critical for guiding GDMT therapy.
Chest X-ray is indicated to assess degree of pulmonary edema, pleural effusions, and cardiomegaly in this patient presenting with dyspnea and bilateral ankle edema consistent with decompensated HF.

Basic metabolic panel is essential given CKD stage 3 comorbidity - need baseline renal function (creatinine, BUN), electrolytes (K+, Na+) before initiating IV diuretic therapy to monitor for electrolyte disturbances and worsening renal function.

Patient has WET and WARM heart failure presentation (bilateral ankle edema, dyspnea on exertion, SpO2 95%). IV furosemide is indicated for decongestion. This is the primary acute treatment for volume overload in heart failure with adequate perfusion.
Troponin should be ordered to evaluate for acute myocardial injury or ACS as a precipitating etiology of new HFrEF diagnosis. Important for risk stratification and guiding further management.

New HFrEF diagnosis requires cardiology consultation for GDMT initiation (ACE-I/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i per AHA guidelines), NYHA class assessment, etiology workup, and long-term management planning. Patient also has CKD stage 3 which requires careful medication titration.

Patient is 'wet and warm' (congested with adequate perfusion, BP 138/82 mmHg, MAP 101). A vasodilator (e.g., IV nitroglycerin) is appropriate to reduce preload and afterload, complement diuretic therapy, and relieve dyspnea in this hypertensive HFrEF patient. Inotropes are not indicated as perfusion is preserved.

Patient has HFrEF with borderline SpO2 (95%) and elevated HR. While currently appearing warm (MAP 101, HR 88), monitoring for cardiogenic shock signs is prudent. This optional action is the only available action in the current phase and should be evaluated given the new HFrEF diagnosis. Patient is not clearly cold/hypoperfused, so this would only be initiated if hemodynamic deterioration is confirmed.

Mandatory action required within 60-minute deadline. Obtaining a comprehensive history is essential for new HFrEF diagnosis — including onset, severity, NYHA class, etiology, and medication history. Not yet completed per the available mandatory list.

Mandatory action required within 60-minute deadline. Physical examination is critical to assess volume status (JVP, edema, lung sounds), perfusion, and hemodynamic profile in this patient with new HFrEF, dyspnea, and bilateral ankle edema.
Mandatory action required within 60-minute deadline. ECG is essential in new HFrEF to identify underlying etiology (ischemia, arrhythmia, LBBB for CRT candidacy), per AHA Heart Failure guidelines.
Mandatory action per AHA HF guidelines. Patient has CKD stage 3 — renal function (BMP) is critical to guide diuretic dosing and GDMT initiation. Overdue per 60-min deadline.
Mandatory action per AHA HF guidelines. BNP/NT-proBNP is essential to confirm heart failure diagnosis, assess severity, and guide management. Overdue.
Mandatory action per AHA HF guidelines. CBC helps identify anemia (a common HF precipitant/comorbidity) and baseline hematologic status. Overdue.

Mandatory action (★) - chest X-ray to assess for pulmonary edema and confirm acute decompensated heart failure findings. Although imaging has been done, this specific action_id is marked mandatory and must be completed.

Mandatory action (★) - TSH is part of initial heart failure workup per AHA guidelines to identify reversible causes of cardiomyopathy (thyroid dysfunction). Patient has new HFrEF diagnosis requiring etiology workup.

Patient is WET and WARM based on presentation (SpO2 95%, BP 138/82, bilateral edema, dyspnea) - formal hemodynamic profile assessment guides treatment decisions including diuresis intensity and need for vasodilators.
AHA guidelines mandate LVEF assessment to confirm HFrEF diagnosis, quantify ejection fraction, guide GDMT initiation, and evaluate device therapy candidacy.
AHA guidelines recommend assessing ICD candidacy in new HFrEF patients; LVEF ≤35% despite GDMT is an indication for primary prevention ICD.
AHA guidelines recommend assessing CRT candidacy in HFrEF patients with reduced EF, particularly those with LBBB or wide QRS, as CRT improves outcomes.
AHA HFrEF guideline requires NYHA class documentation for new HF diagnosis to guide GDMT initiation and therapy intensity. Not yet completed.
Guideline requires assessment of structural abnormalities following echocardiogram to characterize HFrEF etiology and guide management.

AHA guidelines recommend cardiac rehabilitation for stable HFrEF patients to improve functional capacity and quality of life. Patient has bilateral edema and dyspnea on exertion making this relevant for discharge planning.

Patient has bilateral ankle edema and dyspnea consistent with volume overload. Optimizing diuresis for decongestion is indicated per AHA HF guidelines for wet-warm profile, even though IV diuretic was already given — ongoing oral/maintenance diuretic management is needed.

Patient is hypertensive (BP 138/82) with HFrEF and CKD stage 3. Per AHA guidelines, ACE inhibitor/ARB/ARNI is a cornerstone of GDMT for HFrEF and provides afterload reduction; this action addresses hypertension in the context of HFrEF management.

Per AHA HF guidelines, all four pillars of GDMT (ACE/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) are mandatory for HFrEF. Checking GDMT status ensures the patient is on appropriate evidence-based therapy for long-term outcomes.
AHA HFrEF guidelines mandate initiation of ACE inhibitor, ARB, or ARNI as foundational GDMT for HFrEF. Patient has stable BP (138/82) and CKD stage 3 - start at low dose with renal monitoring.
Beta-blocker is mandatory GDMT for HFrEF per AHA guidelines. Patient is hemodynamically stable (HR 88, BP 138/82) with no acute decompensation, making this an appropriate time to initiate.
Confirm that all four pillars of GDMT (ACE/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) are being initiated or planned, and document optimization strategy for this new HFrEF diagnosis.

AHA HFrEF guidelines mandate MRA (e.g., spironolactone/eplerenone) as part of four-pillar GDMT. CKD stage 3 requires caution but is not a contraindication at this stage. This is a key GDMT component not yet initiated.

Patient still has bilateral ankle edema and SpO2 95%, suggesting persistent congestion despite initial diuresis. Adding a thiazide-type diuretic to loop diuretic may improve diuretic response in this CKD stage 3 patient.

Patient has CKD stage 3 and persistent congestion (bilateral ankle edema, dyspnea). Adding metolazone to augment loop diuretic response is appropriate for diuretic resistance in CKD, per AHA HF guidelines for combination diuretic therapy.

AHA HF guidelines recommend ivabradine for HFrEF patients with HR ≥70 bpm in sinus rhythm on maximally tolerated beta-blocker. Patient HR is 88 bpm, making this indication appropriate to assess and potentially initiate.
